    ↳ Why it's tempting: a tolerant parser makes the errors disappear from the logs.
    ↳ What goes wrong: if most responses pass through the repair path, you have a normaliser hiding a quality problem.
    ↳ Do instead: count repairs, alert on the rate, and fix the prompt or enable enforcement.
  • Shelf life: "shape in code, meaning in the prompt" is durable. Which providers enforce schemas, and with what limits, is volatile.

Connections

Path:instruction writingoutput-format specificationJSON mode and schemasparsing and repair loops
  • Builds on prompt anatomy: this is region ④, the one with a twin in code.
  • Owned elsewhere: structured and constrained decoding (LLM-Production) covers how the decoder enforces a schema.
  • Enforced by parsing and repair loops: validate, repair, fail.
  • Used by prompt chaining: each step's output format is the next step's input contract.
  • Drilled in JSON mode, schema or repair.

notes.title: Prompt Chaining — Splitting One Overloaded Prompt into Staged Calls
notes.html:
References

Wu et al. 2021: AI Chains · Anthropic: prompting best practices · Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle · Schulhoff et al. 2024: The Prompt Report

TL;DR

A chain splits one prompt that is doing several jobs into separate calls in an order you fixed, each output feeding the next. Each step gets a small context, its own test, its own retry and possibly a cheaper model. You pay in latency that adds up and reliability that multiplies down, so a chain only wins if each step is more reliable than the single prompt was.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:documentcall 1: extract fields (small model)validate ─fail: retry this step onlycall 2: draft from the fields alone (larger model)validateresult

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a chain buy? Per-step tests and retries, smaller contexts, a model per step.
What does it cost? Added latency, multiplied error, code to run the steps.
Chain vs agent? A chain's steps are fixed by you; an agent picks its next step.

The idea

One prompt reads a 20-page contract, extracts twelve fields, judges three risk questions and drafts a client email. The email is usually fine and the extracted dates are sometimes wrong. You fix the date instruction, and the email's tone changes. You can't improve one job without disturbing the others, and you can't tell from one score which job failed.

That prompt is three steps in one. Extraction needs the whole contract. Drafting needs the twelve fields and nothing else; reading twenty pages it doesn't need only pushes the facts it does need into the middle of a long context.

Split it. Call 1 extracts into a schema and is checked by code. Call 2 drafts from the fields. A bad extraction now re-runs one cheap step, each step has its own eval, and the extraction can run on a smaller model.

Your code decides the order of steps; the model fills each slot. Nothing about the path is left to the model.

The trade: each step is easier and separately testable, and every step you add is one more round trip and one more chance to be wrong.

How it works

The same task as one call and as a chain.

A retry is scoped to the step that failed, which a single prompt can't do.

reliability(chain) = r₁ · r₂ · … · rₙ      ← every step must be right
0.95 · 0.95 · 0.95 ≈ 0.86                  ← three good steps are worse than one 0.92 prompt
0.99 · 0.97        ≈ 0.96                  ← two focused steps beat it

The general derivation is owned by the reliability problem. The practical reading: measure each step, and split only where the split makes the parts more reliable than the whole.

Rule What actually happens
Split along outputs If one response needs two scoring functions, it is two steps.
Pass only what the next step needs The contract between steps is the first step's output format.
Run independent steps in parallel Latency is then the slowest branch, not the sum.

Evolution

Lineage:Oct 2021 AI Chains names the idea2022–23 chaining libraries; chains as the standard fix for weak modelsDec 2024 chaining described as one of several fixed workflow patterns2025 onward strong and reasoning models do more steps inside one call
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly yes. Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) says current models handle most multi-step reasoning internally, and keeps explicit chaining for when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a pipeline. What won't change: a separate step is the only way to test, retry and route one part on its own.
  • Checked on: re-test the single prompt after each major model upgrade; a chain built for an older model may now be dead weight.

Code

One overloaded prompt against the two-step chain.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Read the contract, extract the 12 fields, assess the risks and draft the email. call 1: Extract these fields into the schema. call 2: Draft the email from these fields: {{fields}}
On the input a 20-page contract with two candidate dates a fluent email built on the wrong date; one score for everything step 1 fails validation and is retried; the email is drafted from checked fields
Fails as one failure hidden inside another job —
The one edit — giving extraction its own call and its own check

Measure it

  • Offline: each step's pass rate on its own golden set, and the end-to-end rate, against the single prompt on the same inputs. Ship the chain only if the end-to-end rate rises.
  • In production: retries per step, latency per step and end to end, cost per step. A step whose retry rate climbs is where the next fix goes.
  • Enforced by: the code that runs the steps and the validator between them. Within each step, the prompt is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Chaining splits one mega-prompt into staged calls where each output feeds the next. I do it when one prompt holds several jobs, because each stage gets a focused context, its own eval, its own retry and maybe a cheaper model. The costs are added latency, compounded error and code to run it. A chain is a fixed path I designed; an agent chooses its own.

Q · Mechanism — What tells you a prompt should be chained, not improved? Two signals. The response contains more than one output the system cares about, so the eval needs two scoring functions for one response: that is two steps in one prompt, and improving one risks the other. And the jobs want different context: extraction needs the raw document, drafting needs only the extracted facts. Giving each step only what it needs is usually a bigger gain than any rewording of the combined prompt.

Q · Trade-off — Chaining adds latency and compounds errors. When is one prompt still right? The simpler rung is the single prompt, and it stays right when the task is one job, when latency is the binding limit, or when I have no per-step evals to know whether a split helped. Three steps at 95% are about 86% end to end, so splitting a 92% prompt that way makes things worse. My default is one prompt until an eval shows one job failing on its own; then I split out that job only.

Pitfalls

  • "Chaining improves quality because each prompt is simpler"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: simpler prompts are easier to get right, and each step does look better alone.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: reliability multiplies. Two focused steps at 99% and 97% beat one 92% prompt; three at 95% do not.
    ↳ Think instead: the gain comes from focused context, and has to be measured end to end.
  • Not the same: a chain vs an agent
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both make several model calls for one task.
    ↳ Difference: in a chain your code fixes the steps, so cost is bounded and the path is testable. In an agent the model chooses the next step at run time.
    ↳ Think instead: ask who decides what happens next; see agents vs workflows.
  • Don't chain without per-step evals.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: splitting feels like progress by itself.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you now have more stages and no more visibility, which is harder to debug than the prompt you replaced.
    ↳ Do instead: write each step's test before splitting it out.
  • Don't keep a chain that a stronger model no longer needs.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works, and it took effort to build.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you pay several round trips for something one call now does as well.
    ↳ Do instead: after each model upgrade, score the single prompt against the chain.
  • Shelf life: the multiplication and the scoped retry are durable. How many steps a single call can absorb grows with every model generation.

Connections

Path:output-format specificationprompt chainingself-refine loopsagents vs workflows
  • Builds on output-format specification: the contract between steps.
  • Owned elsewhere: the reliability problem (Agentic) derives the multiplication; agents vs workflows owns the other workflow patterns.
  • Measured by component vs end-to-end eval: green steps and a red result.
  • Costed in latency budget: added round trips.
  • Drilled in one prompt or a chain.

notes.title: Prompt Patterns Catalogue — Names for Structures People Already Used
notes.html:
References

White et al. 2023: A Prompt Pattern Catalog · Schulhoff et al. 2024: The Prompt Report

TL;DR

The catalogue gives prompt structures names, as design patterns did for code, so a team can say "use a flipped interaction here". The names are vocabulary, not evidence that a pattern helps.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
Flipped interaction The model asks you the questions it needs answered before it starts.
Cognitive verifier Break the question into sub-questions, answer each, combine.
Fact-check list List the factual claims separately so they can be checked.

The idea

Six patterns from the catalogue are worth recognising:

Pattern What the prompt asks for Where it lives in this vault
Persona answer as a given role role prompting
Flipped interaction ask me questions until you have what you need requirements gathering, intake bots
Cognitive verifier split into sub-questions, then combine least-to-most
Fact-check list append the claims the answer depends on a hook for an output check
Template fill exactly this skeleton output-format specification
Refusal breaker when declining, say what you can answer instead fallback wording

Treat each as a starting shape to test, not as a technique with a known gain: the catalogue describes and names, it does not measure. For the measured vocabulary of techniques, use The Prompt Report.

Evolution

Lineage:Feb 2023 the catalogue, written for ChatGPTJun 2024 The Prompt Report's taxonomy of techniques. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026) as shared names; several patterns, persona above all, have weaker effects than their popularity suggests.

notes.title: Prompt Anti-Patterns — Four Ways a Prompt Rots
notes.html:
References

Eugene Yan: prompting fundamentals · Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle

TL;DR

Four recurring faults share one cause: prompts only grow. Every clause was added for a reason and nothing ever removes one, unless you prune against an eval.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
Wall of text A long undivided prompt; key rules land in the middle, where they are used least.
Contradictory constraints Two rules that can't both hold; one is dropped and nothing says which.

The idea

Anti-pattern How you recognise it The repair
Wall of text one long paragraph, no regions six regions, delimited
Contradictory constraints a rule that is followed only sometimes read the assembled prompt; delete the loser
Politeness and pleading "please", flattery, "this is very important to my career" delete; it costs tokens on every request and no eval case needs it
Over-stuffed examples a dozen examples, added one incident at a time sweep the count; keep those that move a failure group

The repair that prevents all four is a scheduled pruning pass: remove one clause, re-run the golden set, keep the removal if nothing moves. Diagnosis of a specific failure is the failure taxonomy.
